If there is anything further you want to bring up, it must be settled in a legal assembly.
As it is, we are in danger of being accused of starting a riot because of what happened today. We would not be able to explain this commotion, since there is no good reason for it.
After he had said this, he dismissed the assembly.

19.source: Drafted from the public-domain King James Version, checked verse-by-verse against the Greek text (Strong's Concordance / Blue Letter Bible) for word accuracy. Covers Paul's extended ministry at Ephesus, the disciples who had only known John's baptism receiving the Holy Spirit, the seven sons of Sceva's failed exorcism, the public burning of sorcery scrolls, and the riot of the silversmiths defending the goddess Artemis. All pronouns referring to God, Jesus, and the Holy Spirit are capitalized per this site's standard.

verses.text: When the uproar had ended, Paul sent for the disciples. After encouraging them, he said goodbye and set out for Macedonia.
He traveled through that area, speaking many words of encouragement to the people. Finally, he arrived in Greece,
He stayed there three months. Just as he was about to sail for Syria, he learned that some Jews had made a plan against him. So he decided to go back through Macedonia.

These men went with him: Sopater son of Pyrrhus from Berea, and Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica. Gaius from Derbe went too, and so did Timothy. Tychicus and Trophimus from the province of Asia also went.
These men went on ahead and waited for us at Troas.
But we sailed from Philippi after the Festival of Unleavened Bread. Five days later, we joined the others at Troas, where we stayed seven days.
On the first day of the week, we came together to break bread. Paul spoke to the people. Because he planned to leave the next day, he kept on talking until midnight.
There were many lamps in the upstairs room where we were meeting.

A young man named Eutychus was sitting in a window. He was falling into a deep sleep as Paul kept talking. When he was fast asleep, he fell to the ground from the third floor. They picked him up, and he was dead.
Paul went down, threw himself on the young man, and put his arms around him. He said: Do not be afraid. He is alive!
Then he went upstairs again and broke bread and ate. After talking until daylight, he left.
The people took the young man home alive and were greatly comforted.
We went on ahead to the ship and sailed for Assos, where we were going to take Paul aboard. He had made this arrangement because he was going there on foot.
When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and went on to Mitylene.
The next day we set sail from there and arrived off Chios. The day after that we crossed over to Samos, and on the following day arrived at Miletus.
Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus so he would not spend time in the province of Asia. He was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, if possible, by the day of Pentecost.
From Miletus, Paul sent to Ephesus for the elders of the church.
When they arrived, he said to them: You know how I lived the whole time I was with you. That began on the first day I came into the province of Asia.
I served the Lord with great humility and with tears. I went through hard times because of the plots the Jews made against me.
You know that I never held back from preaching anything that would help you. I taught you in public and from house to house.
I have told both Jews and Greeks that they must turn to God and have faith in our Lord Jesus.
And now the Spirit is compelling me to go to Jerusalem. I do not know what will happen to me there.
I only know that in every city the Holy Spirit warns me that prison and hardships are facing me.
But I do not consider my life worth anything to me. My only goal is to finish the race and complete the task the Lord Jesus gave me. That task is telling people the good news of God's grace.
Now I know that none of you, among whom I have preached about the kingdom, will ever see me again.
So today I tell you that I am not responsible for what happens to any of you.
For I never held back from telling you everything God wants you to know.
Watch over yourselves and over all the group of believers the Holy Spirit has put you in charge of. Be like shepherds to the church of God, which He bought with His own blood.
I know that after I leave, fierce men, like wolves, will come in among you. They will not spare the flock.
Even from among you, some will rise up and twist the truth. They will do this to draw away disciples after themselves.
So be on your guard! Remember that for three years I never stopped warning each of you night and day with tears.
Now I give you over to God and to the word of His grace. This word can build you up and give you a share among all those who are set apart for Him.
I have not wanted anyone's silver or gold or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands of mine have supplied my own needs and the needs of my companions.
In everything I did, I showed you that we must work hard like this to help the weak. Remember the words the Lord Jesus Himself said: It is more blessed to give than to receive.
When Paul had finished speaking, he knelt down with all of them and prayed.
They all wept as they embraced him and kissed him.
What made them saddest was that Paul had said they would never see his face again. Then they went with him to the ship.

20.source: Drafted from the public-domain King James Version, checked verse-by-verse against the Greek text (Strong's Concordance / Blue Letter Bible) for word accuracy. Covers Paul raising Eutychus from the dead after he fell asleep and fell from a third-story window during Paul's long sermon at Troas, and Paul's moving farewell speech to the Ephesian elders at Miletus, including the well-known saying 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.' All pronouns referring to God, Jesus, and the Holy Spirit are capitalized per this site's standard.

verses.text: After we said a hard goodbye to them, we set sail and went straight to Kos. The next day we went to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
We found a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, went on board, and set sail.
We saw Cyprus and passed south of it. Then we sailed on to Syria and landed at Tyre, where our ship was going to unload its cargo.
We found the disciples there and stayed with them for seven days. Through the Spirit, they urged Paul not to go on to Jerusalem.
When it was time to leave, we set out again. All of them, along with their wives and children, walked with us out of the city. There on the beach, we knelt down and prayed.
After saying goodbye to each other, we went aboard the ship, and they returned home.
We continued our trip from Tyre and landed at Ptolemais. There we greeted the brothers and sisters and stayed with them for a day.
The next day we left and reached Caesarea. We stayed at the house of Philip, who preached the good news and was one of the seven men chosen earlier.
He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.
After we had been there a number of days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

Agabus came over to us. He took Paul's belt and tied his own hands and feet with it. Then he said: The Holy Spirit says: In this way, the Jewish leaders in Jerusalem will tie up the owner of this belt. They will hand him over to the non-Jewish people.
When we heard this, we and the people there pleaded with Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answered: Why are you crying and breaking my heart? I am ready not only to be tied up, but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.
When Paul would not change his mind, we gave up and said: Let the Lord's will be done.
After this, we started on our way up to Jerusalem.
Some of the disciples from Caesarea went with us. They brought us to the home of Mnason, where we were to stay. He was a man from Cyprus and one of the first disciples.
When we arrived at Jerusalem, the brothers and sisters received us warmly.
The next day Paul and the rest of us went to see James, and all the elders were present.
Paul greeted them and gave a full report of what God had done among the non-Jewish people through his work.
When they heard this, they praised God. Then they said to Paul: You see, brother, how many thousands of Jews have believed. All of them are very serious about keeping the law.
They have been told that you teach all the Jews who live among the non-Jewish people to turn away from Moses. They say you tell them not to circumcise their children or live by our customs.
What shall we do? They will certainly hear that you have come,
So do what we tell you. There are four men with us who have made a promise to God.

Take these men and join them in the cleansing ceremony. Pay their expenses so they can have their heads shaved. Then everyone will know that these reports about you are not true, and that you yourself obey the law.
As for the non-Jewish believers, we have written to them our decision. They should stay away from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from the meat of strangled animals, and from sexual sin.

The next day, Paul took the men and went through the cleansing ceremony with them. Then he went to the temple to announce the date when the days of cleansing would end, and the offering would be made for each of them.
When the seven days were almost over, some Jews from the province of Asia saw Paul at the temple. They stirred up the whole crowd and grabbed him,

Shouting: Fellow Israelites, help us! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against our people, our law, and this place. He has even brought Greeks into the temple and made this holy place unclean.
They had seen Trophimus, a man from Ephesus, in the city with Paul before. They assumed Paul had brought him into the temple.
The whole city was stirred up, and people came running from every direction. They grabbed Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and right away the gates were shut.
While they were trying to kill him, news reached the commander of the Roman troops that the whole city of Jerusalem was in an uproar.
He at once took some officers and soldiers and ran down to the crowd. When the rioters saw the commander and his soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
The commander came and arrested Paul. He ordered him to be tied up with two chains. Then he asked who Paul was and what he had done.
Some in the crowd shouted one thing, and some shouted another. The commander could not learn the truth because of all the noise. So he ordered that Paul be taken into the fort.
When Paul reached the steps, the mob was so violent that the soldiers had to carry him.
The crowd that followed kept shouting: Get rid of him!
As the soldiers were about to take Paul into the fort, he asked the commander: May I say something to you? The commander replied: Do you speak Greek?
Are you not the Egyptian man who started a revolt some time ago, and led four thousand armed rebels out into the wilderness?
Paul answered: I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no ordinary city. Please let me speak to the people.
After receiving the commander's permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned to the crowd. When they were all silent, he said to them in Aramaic:

21.source: Drafted from the public-domain King James Version, checked verse-by-verse against the Greek text (Strong's Concordance / Blue Letter Bible) for word accuracy. Covers Paul's journey to Jerusalem over repeated warnings including Agabus's dramatic prophecy with the belt, his participation in a purification rite at the temple to ease Jewish concerns, and his arrest and near-lynching in the temple courts, rescued by the Roman commander and his soldiers.

verses.text: Brothers and fathers, listen now as I explain myself.
When they heard him speaking to them in Aramaic, they became very quiet. Then Paul said:

I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but raised in this city. I studied under Gamaliel and was carefully trained in the law of our ancestors. I was just as serious about serving God as any of you are today.
I persecuted the followers of this Way, even to death. I arrested both men and women and threw them into prison,

The high priest and the whole council can tell you this themselves. I even got letters from them to the Jewish leaders in Damascus. I went there to bring these people back to Jerusalem as prisoners, to be punished.
About noon as I came near Damascus, suddenly a bright light from heaven flashed around me.
I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me: Saul! Saul! Why do you persecute me?
I asked: Who are you, Lord? He replied: I am Jesus of Nazareth, the One you are persecuting.
My companions saw the light, but they did not understand the voice of Him who was speaking to me.
I asked: What shall I do, Lord? The Lord said: Get up and go into Damascus. There you will be told everything you have been assigned to do.
My companions led me by the hand into Damascus, because the light had been so bright that it blinded me.
A man named Ananias came to see me. He was a man who carefully obeyed the law, and all the Jews living there respected him greatly.
He stood beside me and said: Brother Saul, receive your sight! And at that very moment I was able to see him.
Then he said: The God of our ancestors has chosen you to know His will. He chose you to see the Righteous One and to hear words from His mouth.
You will be His witness to all people of what you have seen and heard.
And now what are you waiting for? Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name.
When I returned to Jerusalem and was praying at the temple, I fell into a trance
I saw the Lord speaking to me. He said: Quick! Leave Jerusalem right away, because the people here will not accept what you say about me.
I replied: Lord, these people know that I went from one synagogue to another. I put in prison and beat those who believe in You.
And when they killed your follower Stephen, I stood there giving my approval. I even guarded the clothes of those who were killing him.
Then the Lord said to me: Go, for I will send you far away to the non-Jewish people.
The crowd listened to Paul until he said this. Then they raised their voices and shouted: Rid the earth of him! He is not fit to live!
As they were shouting and taking off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air,
The commander ordered that Paul be taken into the fort. He directed that Paul be whipped and questioned, to find out why the people were shouting at him like this.
They stretched him out to whip him. Paul said to the army officer standing there: Is it legal for you to whip a Roman citizen? That man has not even been found guilty!
When the army officer heard this, he went to the commander and reported it. He asked: What are you going to do? This man is a Roman citizen.
The commander went to Paul and asked: Tell me, are you a Roman citizen? Paul answered: Yes, I am.
Then the commander said: I had to pay a lot of money for my citizenship. Paul replied: But I was born a citizen.
Those who were about to question him backed away at once. The commander himself became afraid when he realized that he had put Paul, a Roman citizen, in chains.

The next day, the commander wanted to find out exactly why the Jews were accusing Paul. So he released him and ordered the chief priests and all the members of the council to gather together. Then he brought Paul and had him stand before them.

22.source: Drafted from the public-domain King James Version, checked verse-by-verse against the Greek text (Strong's Concordance / Blue Letter Bible) for word accuracy. Covers Paul's defense speech to the hostile Jerusalem crowd recounting his upbringing, his dramatic conversion on the Damascus road, and his commission to the Gentiles, followed by the crowd's violent reaction and Paul's invoking of his Roman citizenship to avoid an unlawful flogging. All pronouns referring to God, Jesus, and the Lord are capitalized per this site's standard.

verses.text: Paul looked straight at the council and said: My brothers, to this day I have done my duty to God with a clear conscience.
At this the high priest Ananias ordered those standing near Paul to strike him on the mouth.
Then Paul said to him: God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! You sit there to judge me by the law, but you yourself break the law by ordering me to be struck!
Those who were standing near Paul said: How dare you insult God's high priest?
Paul replied: Brothers, I did not realize that he was the high priest, for it is written: Do not speak evil about the ruler of your people.

Paul knew that some of them were Sadducees and others were Pharisees. So he called out in the council: My brothers, I am a Pharisee, and my father was a Pharisee too. I am on trial because I believe the dead will rise again.
When he said this, an argument broke out between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the group was divided.
The Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, and that there are neither angels nor spirits, but the Pharisees believe all these things.
There was a lot of shouting. Some of the teachers of the law who were Pharisees stood up and argued strongly: We find nothing wrong with this man. What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?
The argument became so violent that the commander was afraid Paul would be torn apart by them. He ordered the soldiers to go down, pull Paul away from them by force, and bring him into the fort.
The next night, the Lord stood near Paul and said: Take courage! Just as you have spoken about me in Jerusalem, so you must also speak about me in Rome.
The next morning, some Jews made a secret plan. They made a solemn promise not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul.
More than forty men were involved in this plot.
They went to the chief priests and the elders and said: We have made a solemn promise not to eat anything until we have killed Paul.
So now, you and the council should ask the commander to bring Paul before you. Tell him you want more accurate information about his case. We will be ready to kill him before he even gets here.
But when the son of Paul's sister heard of this plot, he went into the fort and told Paul.
Then Paul called one of the army officers and said: Take this young man to the commander. He has something to tell him.
So he took the young man to the commander. He said: The prisoner Paul sent for me and asked me to bring this young man to you, because he has something to tell you.
The commander took the young man by the hand, drew him aside, and asked: What is it you want to tell me?
He said: Some Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul before the council tomorrow. They will say they want more accurate information about him.

Do not give in to them, because more than forty of them are hiding and waiting to attack him. They have made a solemn promise not to eat or drink until they have killed him. They are ready now, just waiting for you to agree.
The commander sent the young man away with this warning: Do not tell anyone that you have told me this.
Then he called two of his army officers. He ordered them: Get two hundred soldiers ready. Get seventy men on horses and two hundred spearmen ready too. They must go to Caesarea at nine tonight.
Provide horses for Paul so that he may be taken safely to Governor Felix.
He wrote a letter as follows:
Claudius Lysias, to His Excellency, Governor Felix: Greetings.
The Jews seized this man and were about to kill him. But I came with my soldiers and rescued him, because I had learned that he is a Roman citizen.
I wanted to know why they were accusing him, so I brought him before their council.
I found that their accusation had to do with questions about their own law. There was no charge against him that deserved death or prison.
When I learned there was a plot against this man, I sent him to you right away. I also ordered those accusing him to bring their case against him to you.
So the soldiers, carrying out their orders, took Paul with them during the night and brought him as far as Antipatris.
The next day, they let the men on horses go on with Paul, while the rest of the soldiers went back to the fort.
When the men on horses arrived in Caesarea, they delivered the letter to the governor and handed Paul over to him.
The governor read the letter and asked what province he was from. Learning that he was from Cilicia,
He said: I will hear your case when your accusers get here. Then he ordered that Paul be kept under guard in Herod's palace.

23.source: Drafted from the public-domain King James Version, checked verse-by-verse against the Greek text (Strong's Concordance / Blue Letter Bible) for word accuracy. Covers Paul's clash with the high priest and clever appeal to the Pharisee/Sadducee divide before the Sanhedrin, the Lord's night visit encouraging him toward Rome, the 40-man oath-bound assassination plot uncovered by his nephew, and his secret nighttime transfer to Caesarea under heavy armed guard.

verses.text: Five days later, Ananias the high priest went down to Caesarea. He brought some of the elders and a lawyer named Tertullus with him, and they brought their charges against Paul before the governor.
When Paul was called in, Tertullus began his case: We have enjoyed a long time of peace because of you. Your wise planning has brought good changes to this nation.
Everywhere and in every way, most excellent Felix, we accept this with deep thanks.
I do not want to take up too much of your time. Please be kind enough to listen to us for just a little while.
We have found this man to be a troublemaker. He stirs up riots among the Jews all over the world. He is a leader of the group called the Nazarenes,
And he even tried to make the temple unholy. So we grabbed him.
But the commander Lysias came and took him away from us by force,
He ordered those accusing Paul to come to you. If you question Paul yourself, you will be able to learn the truth about all these charges we are bringing against him.
The other Jews joined in and said that these things were true.
When the governor motioned for him to speak, Paul replied: I know that you have been a judge over this nation for a number of years. So I am glad to explain myself.
You can easily check that it was no more than twelve days ago that I went up to Jerusalem to worship.
My accusers did not find me arguing with anyone at the temple, or stirring up a crowd in the synagogues or anywhere else in the city.
And they cannot prove to you the charges they are now making against me.
But I admit that I worship the God of our ancestors as a follower of the Way, which they call a false group. I believe everything that agrees with the Law and that is written in the Prophets,
And I have the same hope in God that these men have. The people who did right will rise from the dead. The people who did wrong will rise too.
So I always work hard to keep my conscience clear before God and people.
After being away for several years, I came to Jerusalem to bring gifts for the poor among my people, and to offer sacrifices.
I had gone through the cleansing ceremony when they found me doing this in the temple courts. There was no crowd with me, and I was not causing any trouble.
But there are some Jews from the province of Asia, who ought to be here before you and bring charges if they have anything against me.
Or let these men who are here say what crime they found in me when I stood before the council,
Unless it was this one thing I shouted while standing among them: I am on trial before you today because I believe the dead will rise.
Felix knew a lot about the Way, so he stopped the hearing there. He said: When Lysias the commander comes, I will decide your case.
He ordered the army officer to keep Paul under guard, but to give him some freedom. He also let Paul's friends come and take care of his needs.
Several days later Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish. He sent for Paul and listened to him as he spoke about faith in Christ Jesus.
As Paul talked about living right, self-control, and the judgment to come, Felix became afraid and said: That is enough for now! You may leave. When it is a good time, I will send for you.
At the same time, Felix was hoping that Paul would offer him money. So he sent for Paul often and talked with him.
When two years had passed, Porcius Festus became governor in place of Felix. But because Felix wanted to please the Jews, he left Paul in prison.

24.source: Drafted from the public-domain King James Version, checked verse-by-verse against the Greek text (Strong's Concordance / Blue Letter Bible) for word accuracy. Covers Paul's trial before Governor Felix, including Tertullus's flattering accusation, Paul's measured defense, and Felix's fear at Paul's preaching mixed with his corrupt hope for a bribe, leaving Paul imprisoned for two years to please the Jewish leaders.

verses.text: Three days after arriving in the province, Festus went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem,
There the chief priests and Jewish leaders came before him and brought their charges against Paul.
They asked Festus, as a favor to them, to have Paul brought to Jerusalem. They were planning to hide and kill Paul along the way.
Festus answered: Paul is being held at Caesarea, and I myself am going there soon.
He said: Let some of your leaders come with me, and bring charges against the man there, if he has done anything wrong.
After spending eight or ten days with them, Festus went down to Caesarea. The next day he opened the court and ordered that Paul be brought before him.
When Paul appeared, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him. They brought many serious charges against him, but they could not prove them.
Then Paul spoke in his own defense: I have done nothing wrong against the Jewish law, or against the temple, or against Caesar.
Festus wanted to do the Jews a favor. So he said to Paul: Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem? Will you stand trial before me there on these charges?
Paul answered: I am now standing before Caesar's court, where I ought to be tried. I have not done any wrong to the Jews, as you yourself know very well.

But if I am guilty of doing anything that deserves death, I do not refuse to die. But if the charges these Jews are bringing against me are not true, no one has the right to hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar!
After Festus had talked it over with his council, he said: You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you will go!
A few days later King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus.
Since they were staying there many days, Festus talked with the king about Paul's case. He said: There is a man here whom Felix left as a prisoner.
When I went to Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews brought charges against him and asked that he be condemned.
I told them that it is not the Roman custom to hand over anyone before he has faced the people accusing him. He must first have a chance to defend himself against the charges.
When they came here with me, I did not delay the case. I opened the court the next day and ordered the man to be brought in.
When his accusers got up to speak, they did not charge him with any of the crimes I had expected.
Instead, they had some arguments with him about their own religion, and about a dead man named Jesus who Paul claimed was alive.
I did not know how to look into matters like this. So I asked Paul if he would be willing to go to Jerusalem and stand trial there on these charges.
But Paul made an appeal to be kept for the emperor's decision. So I ordered that he be kept in custody until I could send him to Caesar.
Then Agrippa said to Festus: I would like to hear this man myself. Festus replied: Tomorrow you will hear him.

The next day, Agrippa and Bernice came with great show. They entered the meeting room with the high-ranking military officers and the important men of the city. At the command of Festus, Paul was brought in.

Festus said: King Agrippa, and all who are here with us, you see this man! The whole Jewish community begged me about him in Jerusalem and here in Caesarea, shouting that he should not live any longer.
I found he had done nothing deserving of death, but because he made his appeal to the Emperor, I decided to send him to Rome.
But I have nothing clear to write to the emperor about him. So I have brought him before all of you, and especially before you, King Agrippa. After this hearing, I hope to have something to write.
For it does not make sense to me to send a prisoner to Rome without stating the charges against him.

25.source: Drafted from the public-domain King James Version, checked verse-by-verse against the Greek text (Strong's Concordance / Blue Letter Bible) for word accuracy. Covers Paul's trial before Festus, his dramatic appeal to Caesar as a Roman citizen (setting the course for the rest of the book toward Rome), and the arrival of King Agrippa and Bernice, setting up Paul's hearing in the next chapter.

verses.text: Then Agrippa said to Paul: You have permission to speak for yourself. So Paul motioned with his hand and began to explain himself:
King Agrippa, I consider myself fortunate to stand before you today, as I explain myself against all the accusations the Jews have made,
This is especially true because you know all about Jewish customs and arguments. So I beg you to listen to me patiently.
The Jewish people all know how I have lived ever since I was a child. They know my life from the beginning, in my own country and also in Jerusalem.
They have known me for a long time. If they are willing, they can tell you that I lived as a Pharisee, in the strictest group of our religion.
And now it is because of my hope in what God has promised our ancestors that I am on trial today.
This is the promise our twelve tribes are hoping to see come true, as they serve God earnestly day and night. King Agrippa, it is because of this hope that these Jews are accusing me.
Why should any of you find it hard to believe that God raises the dead?
I too was convinced that I ought to do all that was possible to oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
And that is what I did in Jerusalem. With the authority of the chief priests, I put many of the Lord's people in prison. When they were put to death, I voted against them.

Many times I went from one synagogue to another to have them punished. I tried to force them to curse the name of Jesus. I was so filled with anger against them that I even went to foreign cities to hurt them there.
On one of these trips, I was going to Damascus with the authority and orders of the chief priests.
About noon, King Agrippa, as I was on the road, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, blazing around me and my companions.
We all fell to the ground. I heard a voice speaking to me in Aramaic: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to fight against me.
Then I asked: Who are you, Lord? The Lord replied: I am Jesus, the One you are persecuting.
Now get up and stand on your feet. I have appeared to you to appoint you as a servant and as a witness. You will tell what you have seen of me and what I will show you.
I will rescue you from your own people and from the non-Jewish people. I am sending you to them,

To open their eyes and turn them from darkness to light. Turn them from the power of Satan to God. Then they may receive forgiveness of sins. They will have a place among those who are set apart for me by faith.
So then, King Agrippa, I did not disobey the vision from heaven.

First I preached to those in Damascus, then to those in Jerusalem and all Judea, and then to the non-Jewish people. I told them they should turn from their sins to God, and show that turning by what they do.
It was for this reason that the Jews grabbed me in the temple courts and tried to kill me.
But God has helped me to this very day. So I stand here and tell my story to everyone, small and great alike. I am saying nothing more than what the prophets and Moses said would happen.
That the Messiah would suffer. He would be the first to rise from the dead, and He would bring the message of light to His own people and to the non-Jewish people.
At this point Festus interrupted Paul as he was explaining himself. He shouted: You are out of your mind, Paul! Your great learning is driving you crazy.
Paul replied: I am not crazy, most excellent Festus. What I am saying is true and makes sense.
The king knows about these things, and I can speak freely to him. I am sure that none of this has escaped his notice, because it was not done off in some hidden corner.
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do.
Then Agrippa said to Paul: Do you think that in such a short time you can convince me to become a Christian?
Paul replied: Short time or long, I pray to God for this. I pray that not only you but all who are listening to me today will become what I am, except for these chains.
The king rose, and with him the governor and Bernice and those sitting with them.
After they left the room, they said to one another: This man is not doing anything that deserves death or prison.
Agrippa said to Festus: This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.

26.source: Drafted from the public-domain King James Version, checked verse-by-verse against the Greek text (Strong's Concordance / Blue Letter Bible) for word accuracy. Covers Paul's eloquent defense before King Agrippa, retelling his Pharisaic upbringing and his Damascus road conversion in the most detail given anywhere in Acts, Festus's outburst that Paul's learning had driven him mad, and Agrippa's famous near-conversion response. All pronouns referring to Jesus as Lord are capitalized per this site's standard.

verses.text: When it was decided that we would sail for Italy, Paul and some other prisoners were handed over to an army officer named Julius. He belonged to a group of soldiers called the Imperial Regiment.
We boarded a ship from Adramyttium about to sail for ports along the coast of the province of Asia, and we put out to sea. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us.
The next day we landed at Sidon. Julius was kind to Paul and let him go to his friends, so they could take care of his needs.
From there we set sail again. We sailed on the sheltered side of Cyprus, because the winds were against us.
When we had sailed across the open sea off the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we landed at Myra in Lycia.
There the army officer found a ship from Alexandria that was sailing for Italy, and he put us on board.
We sailed slowly for many days, and we had trouble even getting to Cnidus. The wind would not let us go the way we planned, so we sailed on the sheltered side of Crete, opposite Salmone.
We moved along the coast with much trouble and came to a place called Fair Havens, near the town of Lasea.
Much time had been lost, and sailing had already become dangerous because by now it was after the Day of Atonement. So Paul warned them,
Men, I can see that this trip is going to bring terrible trouble. We will lose the ship and its cargo, and maybe even our own lives.
But the army officer did not listen to what Paul said. Instead, he followed the advice of the pilot and the owner of the ship.

The harbor was not a good place to spend the winter. So most of the people decided that we should sail on. They hoped to reach Phoenix and spend the winter there. This was a harbor in Crete, facing both southwest and northwest.
When a gentle south wind began to blow, they thought they had gotten what they wanted. So they pulled up the anchor and sailed along the shore of Crete.
Before long, a wind as strong as a hurricane, called the Northeaster, swept down from the island.
The ship was caught by the storm and could not head into the wind, so we gave way to it and were driven along.
As we passed on the sheltered side of a small island called Cauda, we could barely keep the lifeboat safe.

After the men pulled it up onto the ship, they tied ropes under the ship itself to hold it together. They were afraid of running onto the sandbars of Syrtis. So they lowered the anchor to slow the ship down. They let the ship be carried along by the storm.
We took such a violent battering from the storm that the next day they began to throw the cargo overboard.
On the third day, they threw the ship's equipment into the sea with their own hands.
When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and the storm continued raging, we finally gave up all hope of being saved.

After they had gone a long time without food, Paul stood up in front of them. He said: Men, you should have listened to me and not sailed from Crete. Then you would have avoided all this damage and loss.
But now I want you to keep up your courage, because not one of you will be lost. Only the ship will be destroyed.
Last night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve stood beside me
And said: Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar. And God has kindly given you the lives of everyone sailing with you.
So keep up your courage, men, for I have faith in God that it will happen just as He told me.
But we must run aground on some island.
On the fourteenth night we were still being driven across the Adriatic Sea, when about midnight the sailors sensed they were approaching land.
They measured the depth of the water and found it was a hundred and twenty feet deep. A little later they measured again and found it was ninety feet deep.
They were afraid we would be smashed against the rocks. So they dropped four anchors from the back of the ship and prayed for daylight.
The sailors tried to escape from the ship. They let the lifeboat down into the sea, pretending they were going to lower some anchors from the front of the ship.
Then Paul said to the army officer and the soldiers: Unless these men stay with the ship, you cannot be saved.
So the soldiers cut the ropes that held the lifeboat and let it fall away.
Just before dawn, Paul urged them all to eat. He said: For the last fourteen days you have been anxiously waiting, and you have gone without food. You have not eaten anything.
Now I urge you to take some food. You need it to survive. Not one of you will lose a single hair from your head.
After he said this, he took some bread and gave thanks to God in front of them all. Then he broke it and began to eat.
They were all encouraged and ate some food themselves.
Altogether there were two hundred and seventy-six of us on board.
When they had eaten as much as they wanted, they lightened the ship by throwing the grain into the sea.
When daylight came, they did not recognize the land. They saw a bay with a sandy beach. They decided to run the ship aground there if they could.
They cut the anchors loose and left them in the sea. At the same time, they untied the ropes that held the steering oars. Then they raised the front sail to catch the wind, and headed for the beach.
But the ship hit a sandbar and got stuck. The front of the ship stuck fast and would not move, and the back of the ship was broken to pieces by the pounding waves.
The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners to prevent any of them from swimming away and escaping.
But the army officer wanted to save Paul's life, so he stopped them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump into the water first and get to land.
The rest were to get there on planks or on other pieces of the ship. In this way everyone reached land safely.

27.source: Drafted from the public-domain King James Version, checked verse-by-verse against the Greek text (Strong's Concordance / Blue Letter Bible) for word accuracy. Covers the dramatic sea voyage toward Rome, the violent Northeaster storm, Paul's angelic vision assuring that all 276 aboard would survive, and the shipwreck where everyone reached land safely just as promised.

verses.text: Once safely on shore, we found out that the island was called Malta.
The islanders showed us unusual kindness. They built a fire and welcomed us all because it was raining and cold.
Paul gathered a pile of sticks and put them on the fire. The heat drove out a poisonous snake, and it bit onto his hand.
When the islanders saw the snake hanging from his hand, they said to each other: This man must be a murderer. He escaped from the sea, but the goddess Justice will not let him live.
But Paul shook the snake off into the fire and suffered no ill effects.
The people expected him to swell up or suddenly fall dead. But after waiting a long time and seeing that nothing unusual happened to him, they changed their minds and said he was a god.
There was an estate nearby that belonged to Publius, the chief official of the island. He welcomed us to his home and showed us generous hospitality for three days.
His father was sick in bed with fever and a bad stomach illness. Paul went in to see him, prayed, placed his hands on him, and healed him.
When this had happened, the rest of the sick on the island came and were cured.
They honored us in many ways, and when we were ready to sail, they furnished us with the supplies we needed.
After three months, we set sail in a ship that had spent the winter on the island. It was a ship from Alexandria with the carved figures of the twin gods Castor and Pollux on the front.
We put in at Syracuse and stayed there three days.
From there we set sail and arrived at Rhegium. The next day the south wind came up, and on the following day we reached Puteoli.
There we found some brothers and sisters who invited us to spend a week with them. And so we came to Rome.
The believers there had heard that we were coming, and they traveled as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet us. At the sight of these people, Paul thanked God and was encouraged.
When we got to Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him.

Three days later he called together the local Jewish leaders. When they had gathered, he said to them: My brothers, I have done nothing against our people or the customs of our ancestors. But I was arrested in Jerusalem and handed over to the Romans.
They examined me and wanted to release me, because I was not guilty of any crime deserving death.
The Jews objected, so I was compelled to appeal to Caesar. I certainly did not intend to bring any charge against my own people.
For this reason I have asked to see you and talk with you. It is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.
They replied: We have not received any letters from Judea about you. None of our people who have come from there has reported anything bad about you. They have not said anything bad about you either.
But we want to hear what your views are, for we know that people everywhere are talking against this group.

They arranged to meet Paul on a certain day, and came in even larger numbers to the place where he was staying. He told them about the kingdom of God from morning until evening. Using the Law of Moses and the Prophets, he tried to convince them about Jesus.
Some were convinced by what he said, but others would not believe.
They disagreed among themselves. They began to leave after Paul made this final statement: The Holy Spirit spoke the truth to your ancestors. He spoke through Isaiah the prophet when He said:
Go to this people and say: You will be ever hearing but never understanding; you will be ever seeing but never perceiving.

This people's hearts have become stubborn. They can barely hear with their ears, and they have closed their eyes. Otherwise, they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn back to me, and I would heal them.
Therefore I want you to know that God's salvation has been sent to the non-Jewish people, and they will listen!
When he had said these words, the Jews left and had a great argument among themselves.
For two whole years Paul stayed there in his own rented house and welcomed all who came to see him.
He proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance!

28.source: Drafted from the public-domain King James Version, checked verse-by-verse against the Greek text (Strong's Concordance / Blue Letter Bible) for word accuracy. Covers the shipwreck survivors' hospitable reception on Malta (including Paul's survival of the viper bite and his healing ministry there), and Paul's long-awaited arrival in Rome, ending the book with Paul preaching the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ 'with all boldness and without hindrance' -- the deliberately open-ended close of the book. All pronouns referring to the Holy Spirit are capitalized per this site's standard; the 'goddess Justice' in v4 (Greek: Dike) and Paul being called 'a god' in v6 are not capitalized, matching this site's convention that only the true God receives reverential capitalization. This completes the Book of Acts (all 28 chapters).

verses.text: Paul also went back to the towns of Derbe and Lystra. In Lystra there was a believer whose name was Timothy. His mother was a Jew and a believer and his father was a Greek.
The believers in Lystra and Iconium said good things about Timothy.
Paul wanted Timothy to go with him, so Paul circumcised Timothy because of the Jews that lived in those Roman towns. All the Jews knew that Timothy's father was a Greek.

Then Paul and those with him traveled through other cities. Paul and those with him gave the believers the rules and decisions from the apostles and elders in Jerusalem. They told them to obey these rules.
Paul and those traveling with him encouraged the churches to become stronger in their faith, and the number of believers grew every day.
Paul and those traveling with him went to the country of Phrygia and Galatia and they preached there. They wanted to go to the country of Asia, but the Holy Spirit did not allow it.
When Paul and those traveling with him came into the country of Mysia, they tried to go to the country of Bithynia. But the Holy Spirit stopped them again.
Then Paul and those traveling with him went through Mysia and came to the town of Troas.
That night Paul saw a vision. A man from Macedonia came to Paul. The man stood there and begged Paul: Come across to Macedonia and help us.
Paul had seen this vision. So we got ready at once to leave for Macedonia. We understood that God had called us to preach the Good News to the people there.
We sailed from the town of Troas straight to the Island of Samothrace. The next day we arrived at the town of Neapolis.
From there we went to the town of Philippi, a leading city in that part of Macedonia, where the Romans ruled. We stayed there for a few days.
On the Sabbath day we went outside the town to a place by the river, where we thought there would be a place of prayer. We sat down and started to talk to the women who had gathered there.

One of the women listening was Lydia, who sold expensive purple material. Lydia was from the city of Thyatira. Lydia worshiped God, and as Paul spoke, the Lord opened Lydia's heart and Lydia accepted the message that was preached.

Lydia and all the people in her family were baptized. Then Lydia said to us: If you agree that I truly believe in the Lord, then please come to my house and stay there. Lydia asked us again and again until we agreed and went to her home.

One day when we were going to pray, a slave girl met us. She had an evil spirit in her that gave her the power to say what would happen in the future. People paid to listen to her, and she earned a lot of money for her owners.
This slave girl followed Paul and the rest of us, shouting: These men are servants of the Most High God. They will tell you how God can save you.

The slave girl did this for many days, and then Paul became troubled. He turned to the girl and said to the evil spirit: By the power of Jesus Christ, I command you to come out of her! Immediately, the spirit came out.

The owners of the slave girl saw that they would no longer get money from this girl. The owners were angry and they grabbed Paul and Silas and they pulled them into the court, where the leaders of the town were.
The owners told the judge and the leaders: These men are Jews and they are making problems in our town.
Paul and Silas are telling the people to do things that are not right for us as Romans to do.
The whole crowd turned against Paul and Silas. The officials tore the clothes off both men and ordered that they should be beaten.
After the soldiers had beaten Paul and Silas with many stripes, they put them in jail and told the guard to make sure they did not escape.
Then the guard put Paul and Silas in a room deep inside the jail. He put Paul and Silas' feet in blocks of wood.
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing songs to praise God. The other prisoners were listening to them.
Suddenly there was a strong earthquake. The ground and the jail trembled. Immediately all the doors of the jail opened and all the chains of the prisoners fell off.
When the guard woke up and saw that the doors of the jail were open, he took out his sword. He wanted to kill himself because he thought that all the prisoners had run away.
But Paul shouted very loudly and said to him: Do not kill yourself. All of us are here.
The guard asked someone to bring a light and he ran into the room where Paul and Silas were. He trembled and knelt down on the ground in front of Paul and Silas' feet.
The guard took Paul and Silas outside and he asked them: Sirs, what must I do to get saved?
Paul and Silas said to the guard: Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your family.
Paul and Silas told the guard and all the people in his family about the message of the Lord.
The guard took them the same hour and he washed their wounds and sores. Then Paul baptized the guard and all the people in his family.
The guard took them to his house and he gave them food to eat. He and his family were very happy because he now believed in God.
The next morning the Roman leaders sent soldiers to the guard and told him to let Paul and Silas out of jail.
The guard said to Paul: The Roman leaders said that I must let you go free. Come out and go in peace.

But Paul said to the guard: We are Roman citizens. The Roman leaders told the soldiers to beat us where everyone could see it. They put us in jail. But they did not first take us to a court to judge us. Now do they want to send us out secretly? No! Those Roman leaders must come here themselves. They must lead us out.
When the soldiers told the Roman leaders that Paul and Silas were Roman citizens, they became afraid.
The Roman leaders came to the jail and told Paul and Silas that they were very sorry for what they had done. Then they walked with them and asked them to go out of their town.
Paul and Silas walked away from the jail and they went to Lydia's house. There they saw the believers and they encouraged them. Then Paul and Silas went away from the town of Philippi.

16.source: Drafted from the public-domain King James Version, checked against the Greek text (Strong's Concordance / Blue Letter Bible) for word accuracy. A merged/mislabeled verse (9/10, originally tagged as Acts 10:10) has been split apart. Verses 10-18 previously repeated 'Paul and those traveling with him' 3-4 times per sentence; this has been streamlined to match the Greek text's own shift to first-person 'we' in this passage (one of the 'we-passages' in Acts, where the author Luke narrates as a member of the traveling group), returning to third person 'Paul and Silas' from v19 onward to match the Greek's own shift back once the narrative narrows to just the two of them.

verses.text: When they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue.
As was his habit, Paul went into the synagogue. On three Sabbath days he talked with them using the Scriptures,
He explained and proved that the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead. He said: This Jesus I am telling you about is the Messiah.
Some of the Jews were convinced and joined Paul and Silas. So did a large number of God-fearing Greeks and quite a few important women.

But other Jews were jealous. They gathered some troublemakers from the marketplace, formed a mob, and started a riot in the city. They rushed to Jason's house looking for Paul and Silas, wanting to bring them out to the crowd.
But when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some other believers before the city officials. They shouted: These men who have caused trouble all over the world have now come here,
And Jason has welcomed them into his house. They are all breaking Caesar's laws, saying that there is another king, one called Jesus.
When they heard this, the crowd and the city officials were very upset.
Then they made Jason and the others pay money to guarantee good behavior, and let them go.
As soon as it was night, the believers sent Paul and Silas away to Berea. On arriving there, they went to the Jewish synagogue.
Now the Jews in Berea were more open-minded than those in Thessalonica. They received the message eagerly, and they studied the Scriptures every day to see if what Paul said was true.
As a result, many of them believed, as did also a number of prominent Greek women and many Greek men.
When the Jews in Thessalonica learned that Paul was also preaching the word of God in Berea, some of them went there too. They stirred up and upset the crowds.
The believers immediately sent Paul to the coast, but Silas and Timothy stayed at Berea.
Those who went with Paul brought him to Athens. Then they left, with instructions for Silas and Timothy to join Paul as soon as possible.
While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, he was very troubled to see that the city was full of idols.
So he talked in the synagogue with both Jews and God-fearing Greeks. He also talked every day in the marketplace with whoever was there.

A group of Epicurean and Stoic philosophers began to argue with him. Some of them asked: What is this babbler trying to say? Others said: He seems to be teaching about foreign gods. They said this because Paul was preaching the good news about Jesus and the resurrection.
Then they took Paul and brought him to a meeting of the council of Mars Hill. They said to him: May we know what this new teaching is that you are talking about?
You are bringing some strange ideas to our ears, and we would like to know what they mean.
All the people of Athens and the foreigners who lived there spent their time doing nothing but talking about and listening to the newest ideas.
Paul then stood up in the meeting of the council of Mars Hill and said: People of Athens! I can see that you are very religious in every way.

As I walked around and looked closely at the things you worship, I even found an altar with these words written on it: TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. So you are worshiping something you do not know. Now I am going to tell you about it.
The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth. He does not live in temples built by human hands.
And human hands cannot serve Him, as if He needed anything. In fact, He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.
From one man, God made every nation to live on the whole earth. He decided beforehand the exact times and the exact borders where they would live.
God did this so that they would seek Him. Perhaps they would reach out for Him and find Him. But He is not far from any one of us.
For in Him we live and move and exist, as some of your own poets have said: We are His children.
So since we are God's children, we should not think that God is like an image of gold, silver, or stone. Such images are made by human hands and human ideas.
In the past, God overlooked this kind of ignorance. But now He commands all people everywhere to turn from their sin.
For He has set a day when He will judge the world fairly, through the man He has chosen. God has given proof of this to everyone by raising this man from the dead.
When they heard about people rising from the dead, some of them laughed at Paul. But others said: We want to hear you talk about this again.
After this, Paul left the council.
Some of the people became followers of Paul and believed. Among them was Dionysius, a member of the council of Mars Hill, a woman named Damaris, and a number of others.

17.source: Drafted from the public-domain King James Version, checked verse-by-verse against the Greek text (Strong's Concordance / Blue Letter Bible) for word accuracy. Covers Paul's ministry in Thessalonica and Berea (including the noble Bereans who searched the Scriptures daily), and his famous sermon before the Areopagus in Athens using the altar 'TO AN UNKNOWN GOD' as a bridge to proclaim the true God. All pronouns referring to God are capitalized per this site's standard.

verses.text: Later, Paul left Athens and went to the city of Corinth

There he met a Jewish man named Aquila, who was born in the country of Pontus. But he and his wife, Priscilla, had recently moved to Corinth from Italy. They left Italy because Claudius had given an order for all Jews to leave Rome. Paul went to visit Aquila and Priscilla.
They were tentmakers, the same as Paul, so he stayed with them and worked with them.
Every Sabbath day Paul went to the synagogue and talked with both Jews and Greeks, because he wanted them all to believe in Jesus.
When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul spent all his time preaching, telling the Jews that Jesus was the Christ.

But when the Jews opposed Paul and insulted him, Paul shook the dust from his clothes. He said to them: If you are not saved, it will be your own fault! I have done all I can do. After this I will go only to the non-Jewish people.
Then Paul went, and he stayed in the house of a man named Titius Justus, who also worshipped the true God. His house was next to the synagogue.
Crispus was the leader of that synagogue. He and all the people living in his house believed in Jesus. Many other people in Corinth listened to Paul. They, too, believed and were baptized.
That night, Paul had a vision. The Lord said to him: Do not be afraid. You must keep on telling the people about me. You must not stop.
I am with you, and no one will be able to hurt you. Many of my people are in this city.
Paul stayed there for a year and a half teaching God's message to the people.
During the time that Gallio was the governor of Achaia, they grabbed Paul and took him to court.
They said to Gallio: This man is teaching people to worship God in a way that is against our law!
Paul was ready to say something, but Gallio spoke to the Jews first. He said: I would listen to you if your complaint was about a crime or other wrong.
But you argue with each other about words and names and about your own laws. You must decide what is right and what is wrong. I will not judge things like this.
So Gallio made them leave the court.
Then they all grabbed Sosthenes, the leader of the synagogue. They beat him before the court. But Gallio did not worry about that.
Paul stayed with the believers for a long time. Then he left and sailed for Syria. Priscilla and Aquila were also with him. In Cenchrea Paul cut off his hair, because he had made a promise to God.
Then they went to the city of Ephesus, where Paul left Priscilla and Aquila. While Paul was in Ephesus, he went into the synagogue and talked with the Jews.
They asked him to stay longer, but he refused.
He left them and said: I must go to Jerusalem for the feast. I will come back to you again if God wants me to. Then he sailed away from Ephesus.
When Paul arrived at Caesarea, he went to Jerusalem and visited the church there. After that he went to Antioch.

Paul stayed in Antioch for a while. Then he left there and went through the countries of Galatia and Phrygia. He traveled from town to town in these countries, helping the followers of Jesus grow stronger in their faith.
There was a Jew who came to the city of Ephesus. His name was Apollos. He was born in the city of Alexandria, and he was an educated man who knew the Scriptures well.
He had been taught about the Lord and was always excited to talk to people about Jesus. But he only knew about the baptism that John taught.
Apollos started to preach in the synagogue. He was not afraid to speak boldly. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him speak, they took him to their home and helped him understand the way of God better.

Apollos was sent to go to Achaia. So the believers in Ephesus wrote a letter to the believers in Achaia and asked them to accept Apollos. When he arrived there, he was a great help to those who had believed in Jesus because of God's grace.
He argued very strongly against the Jews before all the people. He clearly proved that the Jews were wrong. He used the Scriptures and showed that Jesus is the Messiah.

18.source: Drafted from the public-domain King James Version, checked against the Greek text (Strong's Concordance / Blue Letter Bible) for word accuracy. Verse 5, previously missing entirely, has been restored, and several garbled/fragment sentences (v6, v26) and grammar issues fixed.
